name: Recomp

card.summary: Body recomposition: losing fat and gaining muscle at the same time, mostly discussed for beginners and skinny-fat lifters.
card.note: Forum threads also discuss drug-assisted recomp, which carries separate risks.

quick.overview:
Recomp, short for body recomposition, is the attempt to lose fat and add muscle at the same time, usually by eating near maintenance with resistance training and high protein. Forum posters most often discuss it for skinny-fat people who want a leaner look without a separate bulk and cut.

Threads range from natural diet and training plans to drug-assisted approaches. Some users advise against it and recommend alternating phases instead.
quick.mechanism: Calories are held around maintenance or a slight deficit while lifting and protein intake support muscle retention or gain. Forum users calculate calorie and macro targets week by week.
quick.risks: The sources examined contain no clinical studies. Appetite-suppressing or fat-loss drugs mentioned alongside recomp in forums carry their own medical risks and are not endorsed here. Slow, hard-to-measure progress is the main practical caveat users cite.

lead: Recomp, short for body recomposition, is the attempt to reduce body fat and build muscle at the same time, in contrast with alternating a bulk and a cut.[1][2] It is discussed on looksmaxxing forums mainly in relation to skinny-fat bodies, where a person has low muscle and relatively high fat.[2]

Posters ask for week-by-week calorie and macronutrient plans, discuss modest deficits with intermittent fasting and high protein, and debate whether recomp is a sensible approach compared with a dedicated bulk or cut.[2][3] Some threads discuss using fat-loss drugs and supplements to recomp while bulking.[4]

Bodybuilding references describe bulking and cutting as separate phases with a surplus and a deficit, and note a clean bulk aims to add muscle with little fat, an approach that overlaps with recomp ideas.[1]
infobox: Lose fat and gain muscle concurrently

paras: Recomp aims to change body composition without large changes in weight. It is typically contrasted with bulking in a surplus and cutting in a deficit, which Wikipedia describes as the usual alternating phases in bodybuilding.[1]

One long guide addressed to skinny-fat and overweight people argues against recomposing and recommends an alternative sequence, and invites readers who are not in those groups to read it anyway.[2] Another poster seeking a plan to reach 10 percent body fat naturally describes a 350 kcal daily deficit with intermittent fasting and about 1.2 g of protein per kg, losing 13 pounds in three months.[3]

A third thread asks whether L-carnitine and retatrutide can allow recomposition while bulking. Replies say retatrutide mainly suppresses appetite, making it hard to bulk on, while another says fat burning can occur if intake stays above maintenance.[4]
No studies found in the sources examined for this entry. (Pharmacy-adherence research that shares the name "ReComp" is unrelated.)

lore.intro: Recomp is a recurring question among skinny-fat users who want to look leaner and more muscular without a long bulk and cut.[2][3]

claims.claim: Skinny-fat people should not recomp and should bulk or cut instead
claims.believers: A guide titled to warn against body recomp argues for a different path for skinny-fat and overweight people.[2]
claims.experts: No published trial in the sources examined compares recomp with phased bulking and cutting for appearance outcomes.

claims.claim: Drugs plus L-carnitine allow recomp even while bulking
claims.believers: A poster reports noticeable facial debloating after about ten days of L-carnitine and plans to add retatrutide.[4]
claims.experts: No clinical studies on this combination for appearance were found; replies in the same thread note retatrutide mainly suppresses appetite.[4]

claims.claim: A small daily deficit with high protein can lose fat while keeping muscle
claims.believers: A poster describes losing 13 lb over three months on a roughly 350 kcal deficit and asks for an exact plan.[3]
claims.experts: Bodybuilding encyclopedias say larger deficits raise muscle-loss risk, and describe high protein as part of muscle-preserving cuts.[1]
